claim: D1 medium spiny neurons (MSNs) of the right dorsomedial caudate putamen (CPdm) were chemogenetically excited or inhibited using DREADDs.
source: Here, we focused on understanding how blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) dynamics, measured within a structurally well-defined striato-thalamo-cortical circuit in mice, are shaped by chemogenetically exciting or inhibiting D1 medium spiny neurons (MSNs) of the right dorsomedial caudate putamen (CPdm).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental manipulation performed in the study.

claim: CPdm neuromodulation alters BOLD dynamics within thalamic subregions that project back to dorsomedial striatum.
source: Using a classification approach based on a large and diverse set of time-series properties, we found that CPdm neuromodulation alters BOLD dynamics within thalamic subregions that project back to dorsomedial striatum.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the classification analysis.

claim: Changes in local BOLD dynamics were strongest in unimodal cortical regions and weakened along a hierarchical gradient towards transmodal regions.
source: In the cortex, changes in local dynamics were strongest in unimodal regions (which process information from a single sensory modality) and weakened along a hierarchical gradient towards transmodal regions.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a main finding of the study.

claim: A decrease in functional connectivity was observed only for cortico-striatal connections after D1 excitation.
source: In contrast, a decrease in functional connectivity was observed only for cortico-striatal connections after D1 excitation.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Targeted cellular-level manipulations affect local BOLD dynamics at the macroscale by making BOLD dynamics more predictable over time by increasing its self-correlation structure.
source: Our results show that targeted cellular-level manipulations affect local BOLD dynamics at the macroscale, such as by making BOLD dynamics more predictable over time by increasing its self-correlation structure.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Structural connections constrain functional connectivity, with the strength of this effect varying along a unimodal-to-transmodal cortical gradient in humans.
source: Structural connections have been shown to constrain FC, with the strength of this effect varying along a unimodal-to-transmodal cortical gradient in humans: structure–function coupling is higher for unimodal regions that primarily process information from a single sensory modality than for transmodal regions that integrate information across modalities of large-scale, polysynaptic circuits (Bazinet et al., 2021; Margulies et al., 2016; Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortical gradients exist in mouse and correspond to approximate hierarchical gradients in cytoarchitecture, interneuron cell density, long-range axonal connectivity, and gene expression.
source: Using an MRI-derived biomarker, that is, T1-weighted/T2-weighted ratio (T1w/T2w), which acts as a highly correlated proxy for the structural cortical hierarchy in Burt et al., 2018, Fulcher et al., 2019 have shown that cortical gradients also exist in mouse and correspond to approximate hierarchical gradients in cytoarchitecture, interneuron cell density, long-range axonal connectivity, and gene expression.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Burt et al., 2018 and Fulcher et al., 2019.

claim: Local BOLD dynamics are shaped by structural connectivity, with more strongly connected regions exhibiting slower timescales of BOLD dynamics in mouse and human.
source: Recent work has indicated that local BOLD dynamics are shaped by structural connectivity, with more strongly connected regions exhibiting slower timescales of BOLD dynamics in mouse (Sethi et al., 2017) and human (Fallon et al., 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Sethi et al., 2017 and Fallon et al., 2020.

claim: Time-series properties of the BOLD signal vary with molecular, cellular, and circuit properties of the brain.
source: Time-series properties of the BOLD signal also vary with molecular, cellular, and circuit properties of the brain (Gao et al., 2020; Shafiei et al., 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2020 and Shafiei et al., 2020.

claim: Exciting D1 MSNs with clozapine increased the number of contraversive rotations and decreased the number of ipsiversive rotations compared to controls.
source: Exciting D1 MSNs with clozapine increased the number of contraversive rotations and decreased the number of ipsiversive rotations compared to controls who also received clozapine (MANOVA, Fcontra(1,13) = 19.7, pcontra=0.001; Fipsi(1,13) = 8.8, pipsi=0.01; Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2E and F.

claim: Exciting D1 MSNs increased the total distance moved in the open-field test.
source: Exciting D1 MSNs also increased the total distance moved (MANOVA, F(1,13) = 18.2, p=0.001; Figure 2D).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Inhibiting D1 MSNs of CPdm decreased the number of contraversive rotations and increased the number of ipsiversive rotations when compared to control mice.
source: By contrast, inhibiting D1 MSNs of CPdm decreased the number of contraversive rotations and increased the number of ipsiversive rotations when compared to control mice or to excitatory D1 MSN mice (MANOVA, Fcontra(1,19) = 14.7, pcontra=0.001; Fipsi(1,19) = 66.1, pipsi=1 × 10–5; Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2E and F.

claim: The behavioral results replicate the behavior typically observed for unilateral excitation versus inhibition of D1 MSNs.
source: These results replicate the behavior which is typically observed for unilateral excitation versus inhibition of D1 MSNs (Bay Kønig et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; Runegaard et al., 2019; Tecuapetla et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The balanced classification accuracy for D1 control vs D1 excitation in CPvirus was 75.4% with p-value of 0.02.
source: The balanced classification accuracy for D1 control vs D1 excitation was 75.4% with p-value of 0.02, while for D1 control vs D1 inhibition was 71.1% with p-value of 0.03 (Figure 3A-B).
evidence: The statement presents statistical results from the classification analysis.

claim: The balanced classification accuracy for D1 control vs D1 inhibition in CPvirus was 71.1% with p-value of 0.03.
source: The balanced classification accuracy for D1 control vs D1 excitation was 75.4% with p-value of 0.02, while for D1 control vs D1 inhibition was 71.1% with p-value of 0.03 (Figure 3A-B).
evidence: The statement presents statistical results from the classification analysis.

claim: Changes in classification accuracy for non-transfected subareas of the CP (CPoth) were not significant.
source: By contrast, when we repeated the same approach for the non-transfected subareas of the CP (CPoth), the changes in classification accuracy were not significant.
evidence: The statement presents a negative result from the classification analysis.

claim: Statistically significant classification accuracies were found for multiple thalamic ROIs including parafascicular nuclei (PF), lateral dorsal (LD), lateral posterior (LP), mediodorsal (MD), and ventral and central medial (VM|CM) nuclei of thalamus.
source: We found statistically significant classification accuracies (pcorr<0.05) for multiple thalamic ROIs, that is, parafascicular nuclei (PF), lateral dorsal (LD), lateral posterior (LP), mediodorsal (MD), and ventral and central medial (VM|CM) nuclei of thalamus.
evidence: The statement presents results from the classification analysis of thalamic regions.

claim: ROIs with reciprocal anatomical connections to CPdm displayed higher balanced accuracies than other thalamic ROIs for both D1 excitation versus D1 control and D1 inhibition versus D1 control.
source: Indeed, ROIs with reciprocal anatomical connections to CPdm displayed higher balanced accuracies than other thalamic ROIs for both D1 excitation versus D1 control (two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test, U(8,6) = 0, z = –3.10, p=7 × 10–4, Figure 4B), and D1 inhibition versus D1 control (two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test, U(8,6) = 8, z = –2.07, p=0.04, Figure 4C).
evidence: The statement is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Significant changes in BOLD dynamics after D1 excitation versus control were observed for four cortical ROIs: SSp, VIS, MOp, and PTLp.
source: Significant changes in BOLD dynamics (pcorr<0.05, permutation test) were observed for four cortical ROIs: SSp, primary somatosensory area; VIS, visual area; MOp, primary motor area; and PTLp, posterior parietal association area (Figure 5A).
evidence: The statement presents results from the classification analysis of cortical regions.

claim: Significant changes in BOLD dynamics after D1 inhibition versus control were observed for two cortical regions: PTLp and SSp.
source: Repeating the analysis for D1 inhibition versus control resulted in two significant regions: PTLp and SSp (Figure 5B).
evidence: The statement presents results from the classification analysis of cortical regions.

claim: There is a positive correlation (Spearman's ρ = 0.93, p=0.0001) between cortical ROIs ranked according to the Fulcher et al. multimodal hierarchy and by balanced accuracy for D1 excitation versus D1 control.
source: We find a positive correlation between the two measurements for both types of modulation: (i) D1 excitation versus D1 control (Spearman's ρ = 0.93, p=0.0001, Figure 5C)
evidence: The statement presents a statistical correlation result.

claim: There is a positive correlation (Spearman's ρ = 0.69, p=0.02) between cortical ROIs ranked according to the Fulcher et al. multimodal hierarchy and by balanced accuracy for D1 inhibition versus D1 control.
source: We find a positive correlation between the two measurements for both types of modulation: (i) D1 excitation versus D1 control (Spearman's ρ = 0.93, p=0.0001, Figure 5C) and (ii) D1 inhibition versus D1 control (Spearman's ρ = 0.69, p=0.02, Figure 5D).
evidence: The statement presents a statistical correlation result.

claim: D1 MSN modulation alters a cortical area's BOLD dynamics with a strength that closely follows its hierarchical position, with the strongest response in unimodal areas and the weakest response in transmodal areas.
source: Our results indicate that D1 MSN modulation alters a cortical area's BOLD dynamics with a strength that closely follows its hierarchical position, with the strongest response in unimodal areas and the weakest response in transmodal areas.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: None of the balanced classification accuracies between D1 excitation and D1 inhibition were statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons.
source: None of the balanced classification accuracies were statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons, indicating that activation versus deactivation does not result in significantly distinguishable changes in BOLD dynamics.
evidence: The statement presents a negative result from the classification analysis.

claim: Discriminative individual features were found in two thalamic regions: VM|CM (344 significant features) and LD (284 significant features).
source: Discriminative individual features were found in two regions: (i) VM|CM (344 significant features) and (ii) LD (284 significant features).
evidence: The statement presents results from the feature analysis.

claim: The high-performing features that distinguish D1 excitation from D1 control were directly measuring or sensitive to changes in various types of autocorrelation properties of the BOLD signal.
source: Overall, we found that these high-performing features were directly measuring or sensitive to changes in various types of autocorrelation properties of the BOLD signal.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion from manual inspection of significant features.

claim: The 100 most discriminative features capture a range of time-series features that exhibit high overall similarity to each other as measured by the Spearman correlation distance (1–|ρ| ≤ 0.43).
source: The dendrogram reveals a range of time-series features, derived from different types of methods, that exhibit high overall similarity to each other as measured by the Spearman correlation distance (1–|ρ| ≤ 0.43) on this dataset: from low time-lag linear autocorrelation coefficients, correlation timescale estimates, state-space and AR model fits, properties of the Fourier power spectrum, automutual information, and fluctuation-analysis methods.
evidence: The statement describes results from the dendrogram analysis.

claim: Many individual methods from across time-series analysis that are sensitive to differences in autocorrelation structure are useful for distinguishing D1 stimulation from VM|CM fMRI time series.
source: Overall, our analysis demonstrates that many individual methods from across time-series analysis—which are sensitive to differences in autocorrelation structure (including low-lag autocorrelations and various autocorrelation timescales)—are useful for distinguishing D1 stimulation from VM|CM fMRI time series.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion from the feature analysis.

claim: Positive correlation coefficients between VM|CM and other thalamic, cortical, and striatal regions, which range from ρ = 0.38–0.58, are significant.
source: Results indicate that positive correlation coefficients between VM|CM and other thalamic, cortical, and striatal regions, which range from ρ = 0.38–0.58, are significant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The statement presents statistical correlation results.

claim: D1 excitation causes broadly similar changes to BOLD time-series properties in significant thalamic, cortical, and striatal regions.
source: Overall, these results point towards broadly similar changes in time-series properties after D1 excitation in significant thalamic, cortical, and striatal regions.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion from the correlation analysis of feature scores.

claim: At baseline, ACA, PL, MOp, RSP, GPe, RT, LP, and LD were positively correlated with CPdm.
source: One-sample Wilcoxon tests revealed that ACA, PL, MOp, RSP, GPe, RT, LP, and LD were positively correlated with CPdm, while GPi, VAL|VPM, and VM|CM were negatively correlated (pcorr<0.01, FDR-corrected, Figure 7A).
evidence: The statement presents results from baseline functional connectivity analysis.

claim: At baseline, GPi, VAL|VPM, and VM|CM were negatively correlated with CPdm.
source: One-sample Wilcoxon tests revealed that ACA, PL, MOp, RSP, GPe, RT, LP, and LD were positively correlated with CPdm, while GPi, VAL|VPM, and VM|CM were negatively correlated (pcorr<0.01, FDR-corrected, Figure 7A).
evidence: The statement presents results from baseline functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Direct comparison between D1 excitation and controls indicated a significant decrease in FC after D1 excitation between CPdm–ACA and CPdm–MOp connections.
source: Direct comparison between D1 excitation and controls indicated a significant decrease in FC after D1 excitation between CPdm–ACA and CPdm–MOp connections (pcorr<0.05, FDR-corrected, Figure 7C).
evidence: The statement presents results from functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Excitation of D1 MSNs typically reduced FC, while there was a trend towards increased FC during inhibition, which was statistically significant for FC changes between CPdm and ACA, RSP, and MOp.
source: Additionally, when we compared whether exciting versus inhibiting D1 MSNs differentially affects CPdm connectivity, we saw that excitation typically reduced FC, while there was a trend towards increased FC during inhibition (Figure 7C). This was statistically significant for FC changes between CPdm and ACA, and RSP and MOp (pcorr<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: The statement presents results from functional connectivity analysis.

claim: No significant connections were found in the analysis of DREADD-induced FC changes among all ROIs of striato-thalamo-cortical circuit, including thalamostriatal and thalamo-cortical connections.
source: We also performed an analysis of DREADD-induced FC changes among all ROIs of striato-thalamo-cortical circuit, including thalamostriatal and thalamo-cortical connections, but found no significant connections (pcorr<0.05, FDR-corrected; data not shown).
evidence: The statement presents a negative result from functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Animals which exhibit strong alterations of FC between CPdm and ACA or MOp also exhibit strong behavioral changes (r ≥ 0.681, p<0.0001).
source: We found that animals which exhibit strong alterations of FC between CPdm and ACA or MOp (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B) also exhibit strong behavioral changes (r ≥ 0.681, p<0.0001).
evidence: The statement presents results from correlation analysis between behavior and FC.

claim: The correlation between behavior and FC was not significant for regions with limited FC changes, even if they reached high classification accuracy (r ≤ 0.054, p≥0.768).
source: This was only true for cortical regions whose FC is strongly altered after D1 neuromodulation but not for regions with limited FC changes, even if they reached high classification accuracy (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C and D, r ≤ 0.054, p≥0.768).
evidence: The statement presents results from correlation analysis between behavior and FC.

claim: There is an association between the post-clozapine behavior in an individual mouse and changes in FC between CPdm and the primary motor cortex or anterior cingulate area.
source: This establishes an association between the post-clozapine behavior in an individual mouse and changes in FC between CPdm and the primary motor cortex or anterior cingulate area.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: Modulating D1 MSN activity in the CPdm causes changes in BOLD dynamics which propagate through poly-synaptically connected circuits.
source: Our results provide further evidence that modulating D1 MSN activity in the CPdm seems to cause changes in BOLD dynamics which propagate through poly-synaptically connected circuits.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: CPdm manipulations resulted in BOLD signal perturbations only for thalamic regions with anatomical projections originating in the CPdm.
source: Our CPdm manipulations resulted in BOLD signal perturbations (assessed by significant balanced classification accuracies) only for thalamic regions with anatomical projections originating in the CPdm.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: Thalamic regions with anatomical projections from CPdm displayed more autocorrelated dynamics after neuromodulation.
source: These thalamic regions also displayed more autocorrelated dynamics after neuromodulation, providing causal evidence in support of the strength of incoming projections shaping regional BOLD dynamics.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: Unimodal cortical areas have weaker axonal input strength and fewer integrative functions compared to transmodal regions.
source: Compared to transmodal regions, unimodal regions have weaker axonal input strength (Fulcher et al., 2019) and fewer integrative functions (Wang, 2020; Wang, 2022), which are responsible for integrating inputs from systems implicated in perceiving and acting.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Parvalbumin (PV+) neurons are twice as abundant in unimodal areas than association/transmodal areas, while the opposite is true for somatostatin (SST) neurons.
source: For example, Burt et al., 2018 show that parvalbumin (PV+) neurons are twice as abundant in unimodal areas than association/transmodal areas, while the opposite is true for somatostatin (SST) neurons (Burt et al., 2018; Wang, 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Burt et al., 2018 and Wang, 2020.

claim: PV/SST cell densities strongly vary across a proposed hierarchy of mouse cortical areas, with sensory areas containing a greater proportion of putatively output-modulating PV neurons and transmodal areas containing a greater proportion of putatively input-modulating SST neurons.
source: Kim et al., 2017 have demonstrated that PV/SST cell densities strongly vary across a proposed hierarchy of mouse cortical areas, with sensory areas containing a greater proportion of putatively output-modulating PV neurons and, conversely, transmodal areas containing a greater proportion of putatively input-modulating SST neurons.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: There is a weak but significant relationship between T1w:T2w and the total incoming structural projection strength to a cortical area, with a lower aggregated input weight to unimodal compared to transmodal areas.
source: Some supporting evidence for this hypothesis comes from Fulcher et al., 2019, who found a weak but significant relationship between T1w:T2w (a candidate proxy for hierarchical level; Burt et al., 2018) and the total incoming structural projection strength to a cortical area, with a lower aggregated input weight to unimodal compared to transmodal areas.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Fulcher et al., 2019 and Burt et al., 2018.

claim: An increase in autocorrelation of the BOLD time series was observed for two significant thalamic regions following D1 excitation.
source: An increase in autocorrelation of the BOLD time series was observed for two significant thalamic regions following D1 excitation.
evidence: The statement presents a finding from the time-series analysis.

claim: The time-series features responsible for successful classification indicate an increase in self-correlation structure in the fMRI signal.
source: The time-series features responsible for successful classification indicate an increase in self-correlation structure in the fMRI signal.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion from the feature analysis.

claim: Nakamura et al., 2020 detected an increase in the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) after excitation of D1 MSNs in the dorsal CP.
source: Specifically, Nakamura et al., 2020 detected an increase in the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) after excitation of D1 MSNs in the dorsal CP, which is in line with our own results that revealed an increase in low-frequency power, albeit in thalamic regions.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2020.

claim: Regional differences in temporal autocorrelation of the human cortex are shaped by molecular and cellular properties of cortical regions.
source: Moreover, Shafiei et al., 2020 report that regional differences in temporal autocorrelation of the human cortex are shaped by molecular and cellular properties of cortical regions.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Shafiei et al., 2020.

claim: Cellular excitation of D1 MSNs shapes the temporal autocorrelation of anatomically connected regions at the macroscale.
source: Following this notion, our results provide causal evidence that cellular excitation of D1 MSNs shapes the temporal autocorrelation of anatomically connected regions at the macroscale.
evidence: The statement is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: Different brain regions exhibit varied timescales of fluctuations in neuronal population activity, that is, magnitude of autocorrelation.
source: Assessment of neuronal spike-count autocorrelation has shown that different regions exhibit varied timescales of fluctuations in neuronal population activity, that is, magnitude of autocorrelation (Churchland et al., 2011; Murray et al., 2014), which varied in the presence of a stimulus or a task (Nougaret et al., 2021; Runyan et al., 2017; Wasmuht et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Increased autocorrelation has been observed in parietal cortex neurons following an auditory decision-making task in mice.
source: Using calcium imaging, increased autocorrelation has been observed in parietal cortex neurons following an auditory decision-making task in mice (Runyan et al., 2017), indicating that autocorrelation may be a statistical property that enables information coding by neuronal populations over different timescales.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Runyan et al., 2017.

claim: The variability of the magnitude of the autocorrelation of intrinsic neural signal was demonstrated using resting-state fMRI data and human intracranial recordings.
source: The variability of the magnitude of the autocorrelation of intrinsic neural signal was also demonstrated using other neuroimaging modalities such as resting-state fMRI data and human intracranial recordings (Gao et al., 2020; Stephens et al., 2013; Watanabe et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: D1 CPdm neuromodulation alters neuronal autocorrelation at the population level, shaping the dynamics of the fMRI signal.
source: Based on this, we speculate that D1 CPdm neuromodulation alters neuronal autocorrelation at the population level, shaping the dynamics of the fMRI signal, which is also characterized by an increase in autocorrelated fluctuations.
evidence: The statement is presented as speculation based on the results.

claim: Nakamura and colleagues found that neuromodulation increased delta power in dorsal striatum but not in motor cortex.
source: Nakamura and colleagues have performed electrophysiological recordings in both dorsal striatum and motor cortex before and after D1 MSN excitation. Results indicate that neuromodulation increased delta power in dorsal striatum but not in motor cortex (Nakamura et al., 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2020.

claim: Slow oscillations of delta-band fluctuations contribute to FC and are characterized by brain-wide synchrony.
source: Since slow oscillations of delta-band fluctuations contribute to FC (Wang et al., 2012) and are characterized by brain-wide synchrony (Pan et al., 2013; Uhlhaas et al., 2010), we speculate that differences in low-frequency power changes between the neuromodulated CPdm and cortex contribute to our observations of decreased striato-cortical FC after exciting D1 MSNs.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2012, Pan et al., 2013, and Uhlhaas et al., 2010.

claim: Low power coherence between chemogenetically inhibited areas and remote non-neuromodulated areas contributes to shaping FC between those regions.
source: Moreover, recent findings illustrate that low power coherence between chemogenetically inhibited areas and remote non-neuromodulated areas also contributes to shaping FC between those regions (Rocchi et al., 2022).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Rocchi et al., 2022.

claim: The activity of D1 MSNs in dorsal striatum is necessary for successful execution of locomotion.
source: This suggests that these striato-cortical connections are associated with executing coordinated movements (Klaus et al., 2017), a finding in line with a number of reports showing that the activity of D1 MSNs in dorsal striatum is necessary for successful execution of locomotion (Badreddine et al., 2022; Barbera et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Klaus et al., 2017, Badreddine et al., 2022, and Barbera et al., 2016.

claim: The regions with the strongest changes in FC to other regions were not the same as the regions whose local dynamics were most affected by stimulation.
source: In this study, the regions with the strongest changes in FC to other regions were not the same as the regions whose local dynamics were most affected by stimulation.
evidence: The statement is an observation from the results.

claim: Studies from prior work have illustrated rather weak connectivity of thalamic regions with cortical and striatal regions obtained from anesthetized mice.
source: Studies from our prior work have illustrated rather weak connectivity of thalamic regions with cortical and striatal regions obtained from anesthetized mice (Grandjean et al., 2017), even after cortical neuromodulation (Markicevic et al., 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Grandjean et al., 2017 and Markicevic et al., 2020.

claim: After D1 excitation or D1 inhibition within the dorsal striatum, the firing rates of downstream structures change in a non-uniform manner.
source: While this is at odds with conventional models of the basal ganglia, some studies indicate that after D1 excitation or D1 inhibition within the dorsal striatum, the firing rates of these downstream structures change in a non-uniform manner, that is, with partial firing rate increases and partial decreases within the single structure (Freeze et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2016; Tecuapetla et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Projections from CP to the output nuclei GPi and SNr are topographically segregated so that CPdm projects only to a specific anatomically defined section of GPi/SNr.
source: In addition, a recent tracer study showed that projections from CP to the output nuclei GPi and SNr are topographically segregated so that CPdm projects only to a specific anatomically defined section of GPi/SNr (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Lee et al., 2016 optogenetically activated D1 MSNs in CPdm and observed strong functional activity in cortical sensorimotor areas.
source: For example, Lee et al., 2016 optogenetically activated D1 MSNs in CPdm (i.e., the same target area as in the present study) and observed strong functional activity in cortical sensorimotor areas.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: CPdm projects to specific thalamic nuclei which, in turn, project to unimodal cortical areas including primary motor and somatosensory cortex.
source: This discrepancy might be explained by striato-thalamo-cortical projection where recent studies have shown that CPdm projects to specific thalamic nuclei which, in turn, project to unimodal cortical areas including primary motor and somatosensory cortex (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The statement is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: D1 inhibition at the dorsomedial striatum using DREADDs induces rotational behavior, which is directly proportional to the spatial extent of the viral expression.
source: Bay Kønig et al., 2019 have recently shown that D1 inhibition at the dorsomedial striatum using DREADDs induces rotational behavior, which is directly proportional to the spatial extent of the viral expression.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Bay Kønig et al., 2019.

claim: A total of 38 mice were used in the experiment, aged 16.2 ± 2.8 wk and weighing 24.9 ± 3.3 g at the day of the surgery.
source: A total of 38 mice were used in the experiment, aged 16.2 ± 2.8 wk and weighing 24.9 ± 3.3 g at the day of the surgery.
evidence: The statement describes the experimental subjects.

claim: 950 nL of double-floxed inverted (DIO) recombinant AAV8 virus was used to express either hM3Dq-mCherry (excitatory DREADD, n = 13, eight females) or hM4Di-mCherry (inhibitory DREADD, n = 15, seven females) or mCherry (control, n = 10, six females).
source: Then, 950 nL of double-floxed inverted (DIO) recombinant AAV8 virus was used to express either hM3Dq-mCherry (excitatory DREADD, n = 13, eight females) or hM4Di-mCherry (inhibitory DREADD, n = 15, seven females) or mCherry (control, n = 10, six females).
evidence: The statement describes the experimental procedure.

claim: To activate the DREADD, clozapine was intraperitoneally injected at a dose of 30 µg/kg, 10 min before the start of the behavioral recording.
source: To activate the DREADD, clozapine was intraperitoneally injected at a dose of 30 µg/kg, 10 min before the start of the recording.
evidence: The statement describes the experimental procedure.

claim: A total of 32 mice underwent an open-field behavioral test and each recording lasted 25 min.
source: A total of 32 mice underwent an open-field behavioral test and each recording lasted 25 min.
evidence: The statement describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Resting-state fMRI measurements were obtained with a 7T Bruker BioSpec scanner equipped with a Pharmascan magnet and a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) receive-only cryogenic coil.
source: Resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) measurements were obtained with a 7T Bruker BioSpec scanner equipped with a Pharmascan magnet and a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) receive-only cryogenic coil (Bruker BioSpin AG, Fällanden, Switzerland) in combination with a linearly polarized room temperature volume resonator for rf transmission.
evidence: The statement describes the experimental equipment.

claim: For fMRI recordings, an echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence was used with repetition time TR = 1 s, echo time TE = 15 ms, flip angle = 60°, matrix size = 90 × 50, in-plane resolution = 0.2 × 0.2 mm2, number of slices = 20, slice thickness = 0.4 mm, 2280 volumes for a total scan of 38 min.
source: For fMRI recordings, an echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence was used with the following acquisition parameters: repetition time TR = 1 s, echo time TE = 15 ms, flip angle = 60°, matrix size = 90 × 50, in-plane resolution = 0.2 × 0.2 mm2, number of slices = 20, slice thickness = 0.4 mm, 2280 volumes for a total scan of 38 min.
evidence: The statement describes the experimental parameters.

claim: Clozapine was intravenously injected 15 min after the scan start at a dose of 30 µg/kg.
source: Clozapine was intravenously injected 15 min after the scan start at a dose of 30 µg/kg and a total of 38 D1Cre animals (10 controls, 13 D1 excitatory, and 15 D1 inhibitory mice) were scanned.
evidence: The statement describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (AMBCA) was used to map out the structural connectome of the striato-thalamo-cortical circuit containing the striatal target area CPdm.
source: The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (AMBCA) (Oh et al., 2014) was used to map out the structural connectome of the striato-thalamo-cortical circuit containing our striatal target area CPdm.
evidence: The statement describes the method used for defining ROIs.

claim: The mesoscale structural connectome of the mouse brain was derived from 469 viral microinjection experiments in the right hemisphere of C57BL/6J mice.
source: The mesoscale structural connectome of the mouse brain was derived from 469 viral microinjection experiments in the right hemisphere of C57BL/6J mice.
